newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Izetbegovic raised war crimes issue in U.S. visit.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic raised war crimes issue in U.S. visit.

text.p: The chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, said on Thursday U.S. officials gave him no specific promises to arrest war crimes suspects still at large in former Yugoslavia.
Izetbegovic told Bosnian state television after returning from a visit to Washington that the United States was examining its options on the war crimes issue.
"No one (in Washington) would reveal exactly what they would do. But I think I am not wrong to say that something will be done," Izetbegovic said.
"They assured me that they are considering possible options," he said, without elaborating.

Izetbegovic, the Moslem member of the three-man presidency, said he told U.S. officials that failure to arrest suspects indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia was undermining efforts at building a lasting peace.
"I only said that if you had caught war criminals last year we would have had a completely different situation," he said.
If the suspects had been arrested, Izetbegovic said there would have been no need to extend the mandate for the expensive NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) to keep the peace in Bosnia.
SFOR, which succeeded a one-year NATO-led deployment, has an 18-month mission which expires in mid-1998. Some 8,000 American troops are serving in the multinational force.
Former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and army commander Ratko Mladic are the two most prominent suspects who have refused to face charges before the U.N. tribunal in the Hague.

Karadzic, who was forced to step down as Bosnian Serb president under internationl pressure, has sought to retain his political influence and encouraged the obstruction of the Dayton peace agreement, diplomats say.
Izetbegovic and human rights workers say prosecuting war crimes suspects is vital to building reconciliation between Bosnia's Serbs, Moslems and Croats.
But NATO, reluctant to provoke a local backlash or risk possible casualties, has ruled out launching any "manhunts" for indicted war criminals.
U.S. officials have sometimes spoken of forming a special international force to nab suspects but no details have emerged. Military analysts have dismissed the suggestion as mere political posturing.
